newsitem.title: GERMANY: German labour office calls for jobs programme.
newsitem.headline: German labour office calls for jobs programme.

text.p: The head of Germany's Federal Labour Office on Monday urged Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government to introduce measures to promote investment, as reports surfaced that unemployment reached a post-war record last month.
Labour Office president Berhard Jagoda told the daily Bild newspaper there would be a "rude awakening" in Germany if the government stood idly by while joblessness continued to soar.

A weekend report in the weekly Bild am Sonntag newspaper said German unemployment hit 4.8 million in February topping the record 4.66 million of the previous month. It would be the highest level since the Great Depression of the 1930s.

"I cannot confirm this number and I consider it unlikely," said Jagoda in an interview published in Bild on Monday. "But I fear that one day there will be a rude awakening if we do not soon get a handle on unemployment."
The government has predicted that unemployment levels would peak later this year.
The main opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have said that unless something was done to stop spiralling joblessness, there could be social unrest and a new wave of far-rightist activity.
Corporate profits have climbed in Germany, but industry has been investing more in jobs abroad than at home, citing the need to be in foreign markets and the high costs of German labour.
Under voter pressure to fight joblessness, Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU) and Free Democrats (FDP) have been holding talks with the SPD on tax cuts to boost investment.
Jagoda urged the government to use the traditional economic pick-up in the spring to introduce measures that would promote investment and force a turnaround on the labour market.

More than 300,000 of the current jobless were only interested in working part time, but there were unsatisfactory conditions for hiring part-time workers, he said, adding that improving conditions for hiring could boost job creation.
"It is essential now to promote more investment," he said. "A programme to boost investment could indeed stimulate job creation."

Jagoda said the Labour Office could require an additional three billion marks to finance unemployment benefits and jobs programmes if unemployment, as forecast, hit an average of nearly 4.2 million this year.
"These additional costs must be offset by the federal government," he said.
